newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Chechen commander says Russians prisoners of war.
newsitem.headline: Chechen commander says Russians prisoners of war.

text.p: A Chechen rebel commander holding 21 Russian Interior Ministry troops captive said on Sunday he considered them prisoners of war and had not decided when to free them.

Asked when he would release the Russians, field commander Salman Raduyev told Reuters, "I will think about it...I do not consider them hostages, they are prisoners of war and I consider their weapons to be trophies."
Russian officials had earlier warned Chechen separatist leaders that the detention of the Russian servicemen could halt Moscow's military withdrawal from the region.

Up to 60 armed Chechen fighters arriving by car and bus seized the Russians on Saturday near the border between Chechnya and the region of Dagestan, Russian Interior Ministry spokesman Arkady Pashtushkov said.

Raduyev's spokeswoman earlier told reporters in the Chechen capital Grozny the captives would be released on Sunday. First Deputy Prime Minister in the Chechen government Movladi Udugov said they would be released on Monday.
"The Russian policemen will be handed over to the Russian aucthorities tomorrow," Udugov told NTV commercial television. He said their lives were not in danger.
Raduyev said his soldiers seized the Russians after they had stopped his men on the road to Dagestan where they had been invited to attend a conference.
He had given the order to seize the troops and disarm them after the Russians had ordered his men to give up their weapons.
He called on the Russian military command and the Dagestani authorities to apologise for the incident and said he would hand over the "prisoners" via Chechen leaders in Dagestan.

Raduyev led a hostage-taking raid into Dagestan last January, prompting a large-scale Russian military rescue effort during which 26 Russians and about 150 Chechens died. The Chechen military leader escaped badly wounded.
Two years after it launched a full-scale military assault on Chechnya to quash the region's moves towards independence, Russia last month agreed to pull out its remaining troops from the region.

Three top Russian officials in the region overseeing Chechen policy sent Chechnya's president a memorandum warning that unless the Russians were released, Moscow could halt the withdrawal of its forces, Interfax news agency said.

"These provocations could have irreparable consequences that could lead up to stopping the withdrawal of federal forces and the peace process in Chechnya as a whole," the agency quoted the document as saying.
Government officials in Moscow said they could not immediately confirm details of the memorandum.

Chechen leaders, anxious to ensure that Russian troops leave the region before a general election scheduled for January 27, have denounced similar incidents in the past and moved to resolve them quickly.
Interior Ministry troops commander Anatoly Shkirko said the Chechens used women and children to help disarm the Russians, preventing them from opening fire, RIA news agency said.

Russia sent forces into Chechnya in December 1994 to crush an independence bid, but the military failed to win control of the region and are now pulling out. Tens of thousands of people, mostly civilians, were killed in 21 months of fighting.
